study.title: Psalm 111 Praise to God as the Way of Wisdom
study.overview: This psalm of praise presents the works of the LORD as the basis for worshiping and learning it. The text binds God's greatness to his righteousness, mercy, fidelity to the covenant, provision for his people, and a ransom granted to him. The final verse concentrates the message: the fear of the LORD is not a servile fear, but obedient reverence that inaugurates true wisdom and produces lasting understanding. Thus, the psalm teaches that knowing God is not only to admire his deeds, but to respond to them with praise, obedience and fidelity.

outline.title: Personal Praise based on God's grandiose works
outline.explanation: The psalmist declares his decision to praise the LORD with all his heart, both in the midst of the righteous and in the congregation. Then he draws attention to the great, glorious and memorable works of God, who reveal his righteous, merciful and godly character. The focus is not only on what God does, but in who he is, for his actions manifest his glory and his permanent justice.

outline.title: Permanent Provision, Alliance and Loyalty
outline.explanation: Here the psalm highlights God's attention to the needs of his people, including food, and his constant remembrance of the covenant. He also states that he showed the power of his works by granting his people an inheritance, and that all that their hands do is truth and judgment. His commandments are firm, made in truth and righteousness, indicating that God's rule is trustworthy and morally upright.

outline.title: Rescue, holiness and the principle of wisdom
outline.explanation: The psalm culminates in the ransom given to the people and in the establishment of the covenant forever, showing that redemption is a central part of divine action. The name of God is holy and fearful, that is, worthy of reverence. Therefore wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD; those who practice this reverence are called intelligent, and praise to God abides forever.

study.context: The text is presented as a psalm of praise and wisdom. The notes indicate that he belongs to the group of psalms that repeat the call to praise the LORD and that is at the same time a reflection on the acts of God. References to the covenant, food, inheritance and rescue show that the psalmist recalls God's action in favor of his people, without relying on historical details beyond what the poem itself mentions. Some readings of the notes associate the psalm with the celebration of God's works in favor of Israel, but this should be understood as interpretation, not as explicitly stated in each verse.
study.theology: The psalm unites worship and wisdom. Instead of treating wisdom as a mere accumulation of information, he defines it as a posture of obedient reverence before the LORD. The justice, mercy, faithfulness, and holiness of God are not abstractions; they appear in their concrete acts of provision, covenant, redemption, and moral rule. The people of God are called not only to recognize these works, but to live in a way consistent with them, because receiving the benefits of the covenant implies ethical responsibility. The verse 10 summarizes the theology of the psalm: the true intelligence begins when the creature submits with reverent fear to the Creator. Praise, then, is not only an emotional response, but a continuous expression of a life shaped by the wisdom of God.

scholarViews.insight: The commentary understands verse 10 as a teaching that true wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD, linking wisdom to life and reverence.
The note sees the psalm as a psalm of praise in which the psalmist himself serves as an example in deciding to worship God with all his heart, in public and among the righteous.
The commentary highlights that the works of the Lord are great and worthy of investigation, because those who examine them with pleasure end up admiring the perfections of the Creator.

questions: How is my praise to God sustained by an active memory of his works, and not just by momentary emotion?
In which areas of life do I need to treat the fear of the LORD as the beginning of wisdom, and not as a secondary religious detail?
How should the remembrance that God be faithful to his covenant should mold my obedience, my decisions, and my use of the word?
study.practice: Set aside a time to list concrete works of God in your life, in the church and in the history of redemption, and turn that remembrance into a prayer of praise. Then choose a practical attitude of obedient reverence for the week, such as abandoning an inconsistent practice, seeking integrity in words, or serving someone with gratitude. Read the whole psalm aloud and highlight the deeds of God's action and the human answers that the text requires.
study.uncertainty: The given notes suggest possible historical associations of the psalm with the life of Israel and, in a reading, with the post-exile restoration, but this is not explicitly stated in the biblical text and should be treated only as interpretation. There is also no basis for notes to safely identify the exact occasion of the composition.
